paragraphs.text: Greenhouse gases make the Earth send its heat to space from high, cold air instead of from the warm surface...
The rest of this page puts numbers on each step.
Start from conservation of energy... energy balance.
Sunlight delivers 1361 W/m² to a panel that faces the Sun.
The Earth catches sunlight on a disc of area πR², but it emits from its whole sphere...
The albedo is the fraction of sunlight... 240 W/m².
The division by 4 matters. Without it, the calculation below gives 360 K...
leap: "the calculation below gives 360 K": this points ahead to a calculation the reader has not seen yet, so they cannot check the number at this point

paragraphs.text: A body at temperature T emits σT⁴ watts per square metre...
Set σT⁴ = 240 W/m² and solve: T = 255 K... emission temperature
The measured average surface temperature is 288 K... The greenhouse gases cause that 33 K.
The Sun is hot (about 5800 K)... This is infrared
A greenhouse gas lets most sunlight pass but absorbs and emits infrared...
So sunlight reaches the ground. But infrared from the ground is absorbed by the air...
Infrared reaches space only from air that has little greenhouse gas above it... emission height.
The air at the emission height must emit 240 W/m², so it must be at the emission temperature, 255 K.
The air gets colder with height... the lapse rate.
Height / Temperature: 0 km 288 K, 2 km 275 K, 5 km 255 K
excess: "| 2 km | 275 K |": this row is never used in the argument

paragraphs.text: Now the 33 K has a cause: 255 K + 6.5 K/km × 5 km ≈ 288 K.
Where does the surface's extra emission go? ... The air emits 330 W/m² of infrared down to the surface.
leap: "The air emits 330 W/m² of infrared down to the surface": the figure is given with no reason why it is so large, or why it is larger than the 240 W/m² that leaves the top

paragraphs.text: sunlight 160 | infrared 390; infrared from the air 330 | rising warm air and evaporation 100
leap: "sunlight | 160": §1 said the Earth absorbs 240 W/m², and the text never says where the other 80 W/m² goes (into the air?). The reader stops to reconcile the two figures
The table explains the surface's warmth by downward infrared, but it is not tied back to the emission-height account. The reader may wonder which of the two is the real explanation
excess: The whole surface-budget aside: the main argument (emission height + lapse rate) does not need it

paragraphs.text: Predict first: CO₂ doubles, from its pre-industrial 280 ppm to 560 ppm...
More gas means the infrared must start higher... about 150 m.
The air 150 m higher is about 1 K colder
Colder air emits less... radiative forcing.
The Earth gains energy and warms. The lapse rate holds, so the whole profile warms together.
Warming stops when the air at the new emission height is back at 255 K...
This 1 K counts only this mechanism... about 3 K (IPCC best estimate). Today's 420 ppm already gives a forcing of about 2.2 W/m².
leap: "Today's 420 ppm already gives a forcing of about 2.2 W/m²": the reader cannot get 2.2 from 3.7 per doubling, because the rule that each doubling adds the same forcing does not come until §6

paragraphs.text: The usual picture, "greenhouse gases trap heat like a blanket", says more gas always warms...
Suppose the atmosphere had the same temperature at every height (a lapse rate of 0)...
So the warming depends on two things together...
Near the ground, CO₂ already absorbs almost all infrared at its main wavelength (15 µm)...
leap: "the escape happens high up, where the air is thin": the text does not say why thin air makes the near-ground saturation irrelevant (thin air absorbs less, so it is not saturated there)

paragraphs.text: Energy balance requires the Earth to emit 240 W/m² to space...
Feedbacks in detail...; Why only some molecules absorb infrared...; Why each doubling gives the same forcing...; Where added CO₂ goes...

cuts: The surface-budget aside in §3 (line 54 and the table at lines 56-60) is the biggest cut. It is off the main line, and its 160 W/m² sunlight figure clashes with the 240 W/m² from §1 without explanation. Cut it, or account for the missing 80 W/m² in one clause.
§4 line 73: "Today's 420 ppm already gives a forcing of about 2.2 W/m²." Cut it, or move it to §6 after the per-doubling rule.
§3 table: the 2 km row, which is never used.

question.text: Why does adding gases that absorb infrared make the surface warmer, and by how much?
question.known_at: The title (line 1), and the bold lead (line 5) right after it
question.result_stated: Yes, in words, at line 5: "Greenhouse gases make the Earth send its heat to space from high, cold air instead of from the warm surface. Cold air emits less, so the whole lower atmosphere, and the surface with it, must be warmer before enough energy leaves."

reply.motive: There is a reason for the approach: line 78, "The usual picture, 'greenhouse gases trap heat like a blanket', says more gas always warms. A test case shows that it does not." It comes late, in §5. There is no reason to care about the question near the start. The stakes (CO₂ doubling, "Today's 420 ppm") only appear in §4.
reply.close: Yes. Line 91: "Greenhouse gases move that emitting air up to about 5 km. The lapse rate of 6.5 K/km makes the surface 33 K warmer, at 288 K. More greenhouse gas lifts the emission height and warms the surface." Line 82 also states the general condition: "the gas lifts the emission height, and the air is colder higher up."
reply.recap: Greenhouse gases push the level where Earth's heat escapes to space higher up, into colder air, and because air gets colder with height, the surface has to sit warmer below that level; more CO₂ pushes the level higher and warms the surface more.
reply.strongest: §5 (lines 78-82): the test with a lapse rate of 0 shows that warming needs both a rising emission height and colder air above, which also explains why the blanket picture falls short. §4's numbered chain (lines 67-71) is a close second.
reply.weakest: The §3 surface budget (lines 54-60). Its 160 W/m² sunlight figure contradicts the 240 W/m² from §1 with no explanation, and the section brings in a back-radiation picture that is never tied to the emission-height argument.
suggestions: In the surface budget, say that the air and clouds absorb about 80 W/m² of sunlight directly, so the 160 and 240 figures fit together.
Add one sentence near the top on why this matters, for example: it is how scientists predict the warming from CO₂ that people add.
In §6, say that thin air high up absorbs too little to be saturated, which is why adding gas there still matters.
Spell out IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) at first use.
